# Why this module is built this way

This module asks before it explains, and asks again after you make something. Both choices come from research on how people learn. The sources are below, for anyone who wants them.

{{deeper}}

- Slamecka, N. J., & Graf, P. (1978). The generation effect: Delineation of a phenomenon. *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 4*(6), 592–604. https://doi.org/10.1037/0278-7393.4.6.592. The original demonstration that material a learner produces is remembered better than the same material read.
- Pan, S. C., & Sana, F. (2021). Pretesting versus posttesting: Comparing the pedagogical benefits of errorful generation and retrieval practice. *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 27*(2), 237–257. https://doi.org/10.1037/xap0000345. Guessing before the explanation, even wrongly, helped learners as much as or more than being tested only afterwards.
- Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning. *Psychological Science, 17*(3), 249–255. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x. Pulling an answer back out of memory is itself a learning event. That is the second pass.
- Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. *Psychological Science, 19*(11), 1095–1102. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02209.x. How long to wait before trying again, depending on how long you want to remember. That is why questions come back in later modules.
- Deslauriers, L., McCarty, L. S., Miller, K., Callaghan, K., & Kestin, G. (2019). Measuring actual learning versus feeling of learning in response to being actively engaged in the classroom. *PNAS, 116*(39), 19251–19257. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1821936116. Students in active classes learned more and *felt* they learned less.
- Mayer, R. E. (2020). *Multimedia learning* (3rd ed.). Cambridge University Press. Why every picture here explains something and none is decoration, and why the extra material sits behind "go deeper."
- Wiggins, G., & McTighe, J. (2005). *Understanding by design* (2nd ed.). ASCD. Why the module was planned backward from the assignment, and where "the question to keep asking" comes from.
- Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans. *American Psychologist, 54*(7), 493–503. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.54.7.493. Why the make block asks you to name your two evenings.
